"We now have data broadly defined that says the economy has indeed strengthened," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said in a press conference following the meeting. "Underlying growth is higher. Inflation is the problem. Stable prices have been the problem for, now, more than five and a half years.

"So what the committee decided to do today was take an action to ensure a timely return to our price stability."

Noting that the economy is essentially at full employment, Warsh said he thinks the Fed can tame inflation without depressing growth.

"I don't believe that we need to do harm to the labor markets to achieve our objective," he said. "I don't believe that the two parts of our mandate — price stability and full employment — are working at cross purposes over the medium term."

In their updated summary of economic projections, officials now see one more rate hike this year. That compares with expectations in June, when half of the committee expected they would need to raise rates once this year, while the rest thought they could hold rates steady. Warsh didn't show his hand, declining to participate in the so-called dot plot for the second time.

For 2026, 12 officials see two rate hikes, four see three rate hikes, while two see one rate hike.

The median of 18 Fed officials projects holding rates steady in 2027, after two hikes this year, followed by one cut in 2028.

Headline inflation is now seen rising 3.7%, compared with 3.6% previously. On a "core" basis, officials see inflation at 3.4%, compared with 3.3% previously. Officials don't see inflation dropping back to their 2% goal until after 2028.

The latest Consumer Price Index reading showed prices rose 0.3% in August month over month on a "core" basis, which strips out volatile food and energy prices to better gauge underlying inflation. articles.title: 'Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%': Trump reacts to Fed's rate hike
articles.summary: President Trump reacted to Wednesday's interest rate increase by saying rates "in the United States should be 1%, or less."
articles.body:
President Trump reacted to Wednesday's interest rate increase by saying rates "in the United States should be 1%, or less."

He claimed that "our Country is BOOMING with new Investment" as he discussed the trade deficit as a reason to "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" in a post on Truth Social.

Trump had previously threatened to stop trading with countries that have a trade deficit unless the Fed cuts rates but saw the central bank move in the opposite direction this week.

The White House reaction came after Trump's team tried to telegraph a hands-off approach to the Federal Reserve in recent weeks, but Trump and his team quickly hit back at the decision.

Senior Deputy press secretary Kush Desai also reacted to the move in an appearance on Fox News. Desai said this was a "rather unfortunate decision by the Federal Reserve" that was "not backed by a particularly compelling economic case."

Desai also claimed that the current price increases are "entirely driven by an energy supply shock." That was at odds with Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh, who said Wednesday's action was taken in part to stem wider price increases.

Trump, in the past, has praised Warsh personally but repeatedly called for lower rates and called the Federal Open Market Committee "political" for not lowering rates. Just this past weekend, the president again stated his view that the US should have the lowest interest rates in the world.

Warsh voted along with his colleagues to raise rates but didn't offer a projection about future rate hikes and dodged a question during a press conference on Wednesday afternoon about the White House reaction to the rate hike.

"I've got nothing for you on a discussion with the president," Warsh said.

The first missive from the White House came after the central bank unanimously raised interest rates for the first time in three years and signaled one more rate hike is likely before the end of the year, an acknowledgment that the Fed needed to step in to counteract price pressures.

Appointed by Trump earlier this year, Warsh repeatedly underlined that inflation has remained too high and promised that "this committee will deliver price stability."

Warsh repeatedly dodged politics during a press conference on Wednesday as he called independence of the central bank a two-way street.

"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane, he said. "We'll let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too."

articles.title: More Americans say AI will hurt the environment than help it: Poll
articles.summary: More Americans believe AI will have negative environmental impacts on the upcoming decade than those who think the technology will help the environment, a poll released Wednesday found. In the newly published survey from The Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, 47 percent of respondents predicted AI will do “more to hurt” the environment…
articles.body:
More Americans believe AI will have negative environmental impacts on the upcoming decade than those who think the technology will help the environment, a poll released Wednesday found.

In the newly published survey from The Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, 47 percent of respondents predicted AI will do “more to hurt” the environment over the next 10 years. Fifteen percent said AI would instead do “more to help.”

The report comes as the public grows increasingly skeptical of emerging AI technology, and the issues surrounding it — such as privacy concerns, the construction of large data centers and the lack of federal regulations — become key talking points amid the ongoing midterm election cycle.

Almost a fifth of respondents, 19 percent, said the technology “will not make much difference” when it comes to the environment, while 18 percent were unsure about AI’s impact in this area and 1 percent did not answer the question.

Fears surrounding the environmental impacts of AI appear to be up from last year. In 2025, 33 percent of participants in another AP/NORC study said they thought AI was going to do more harm than good to the environment.

In July, Microsoft reported carbon emissions increased by 25 percent last year, which the company primarily contributed to “the expansion of our datacenter infrastructure.”

“While the decision increases our reported emissions in the near term, it enables us to increase the development of new CFE [carbon-free electricity] rather than relying on certificates alone,” Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith and Chief Sustainability Officer Melanie Nakagawa said in the report.

They added, “We believe this change will create more long-term sustainability benefits. Growth-related emissions pressure was expected.”

The AP/NORC poll, funded by the University of Chicago’s Energy Policy Institute, took place from July 6 and 24. The survey featured 3,424 respondents and had a plus or minus 2.2 percentage point error margin.

articles.title: Warsh says Fed cares ‘very much’ about AI developments
articles.summary: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said Wednesday the central bank is keeping tabs on rapidly developing artificial intelligence (AI) models. “We care very much about what’s happening in artificial intelligence,” Warsh told reporters, after the Federal Open Market Committee raised interest rates by a quarter point. The Fed chair noted he is interested in how…
articles.body:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said Wednesday the central bank is keeping tabs on rapidly developing artificial intelligence (AI) models.

“We care very much about what’s happening in artificial intelligence,” Warsh told reporters , after the Federal Open Market Committee raised interest rates by a quarter point.

The Fed chair noted he is interested in how AI will impact the demand and supply sides of the economy. Roughly 5.8 million American workers are in fields with “high exposure” to displacement from AI, according to a July report from Apollo Global Management.

Warsh also said his task force on AI’s impact on the economy should provide him with a report by the end of the year.

“The policy decisions that are made about the risks and rewards, the challenges and opportunities [of AI], those are decisions made by other parts of the government,” Warsh added. “I’m going to leave it to them to make those … political decisions, those policy decisions.”

Democratic and Republican lawmakers have raised concerns about AI models, after a slew of researchers have warned about their capabilities.

“Do not underestimate the power of this technology. These will soon be superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources,” former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon wrote last week on the social platform X.

Coxon later wrote that those building AI models “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

His former boss, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, called for a slowdown in development days later, arguing it is necessary to allow risk prevention measures to “keep up.”

“Society must have a say in how this technology is used, and more time for the necessary public deliberations — which pacing the frontier would bring us — is surely a good thing,” Amodei wrote in an essay .

Lawmakers from both chambers have introduced various bills to regulate AI, but the House is departing for a seven-week recess on Wednesday.

The Senate, meanwhile, is scheduled to be on recess for nearly all of October and eight days in November. Congress also has multiple political fights ahead, from avoiding a government shutdown in December to passing the annual farm bill .

“Do you think we’re capable of regulating AI? I mean, we can’t pass a budget, you think we’re going to have some great bill on AI?” Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.) told The Hill on Tuesday.

President Trump has taken a softer approach to AI, arguing the U.S. must lead in the race against China and cannot overly regulate the technology.

Trump said Monday the federal government already has “tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power” over AI companies.

“There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China,” the president wrote on Truth Social .

Miranda Nazzarro contributed to this article.

articles.title: Court tosses EPA restrictions on highly toxic paint stripper chemical
articles.summary: A federal appeals court this week threw out an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rule that banned most uses of a highly toxic chemical used as a paint stripper. The EPA has said that the chemical in question, known as methylene chloride (MC), is “likely to be carcinogenic to humans.” When it put forward the rule…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court this week threw out an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rule that banned most uses of a highly toxic chemical used as a paint stripper.

The EPA has said that the chemical in question, known as methylene chloride (MC), is “likely to be carcinogenic to humans.” When it put forward the rule in 2024 , the EPA also said that the substance had caused at least 88 deaths from short-term exposure since 1980.

However, this week, the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals sided with industry challengers to the EPA’s restrictions, saying the agency went too far.

“At every juncture of its scientific analysis, EPA has gone with the most extreme position,” said the opinion , from Reagan appointees Patrick Higginbotham and Edith Jones, as well as George W. Bush appointee Leslie Southwick.

In particular, the judges said that the agency “it discounted relevant human studies despite decades of MC’s use without significant adverse epidemiological findings” and assumed that workers would not use personal protective equipment, among other issues.

They also wrote that the EPA “failed to adequately consider profound economic consequences of its regulation or the limited availability of alternatives that are economically and technically feasible.”

The rule was put forward by the Biden administration. The Trump administration also defended it in court, though it has said it would reconsider parts of the rule, including its assumption that workers would not wear protective equipment.

The American Chemistry Council, a trade group representing the chemical industry, cheered the ruling in a written statement. The group also said that it appreciates “the current EPA’s efforts to bring greater transparency, stakeholder engagement, and regulatory certainty to TSCA [Toxic Substances Control Act] implementation, and this ruling provides an important foundation for that work.”

However, health advocates criticized the court decision.

“This ruling sides with the chemical industry at the expense of public health and will put more people at risk of serious harm, including death from acute exposure, cancer, and kidney and liver toxicity from long-term exposures,” said Liz Hitchcock, director of federal policy at Toxic-Free Future, in a written statement.

articles.title: Trump health nominees face tame Senate hearing: 3 takeaways
articles.summary: Senators heard from three of President Trump’s health nominees on Wednesday, including his third pick to be U.S. surgeon general, with this recent crop seeming to better align with what lawmakers wanted to hear. The Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) held a hearing to go over the nominations of Nicole Saphier…
articles.body:
Senators heard from three of President Trump’s health nominees on Wednesday, including his third pick to be U.S. surgeon general, with this recent crop seeming to better align with what lawmakers wanted to hear.

The Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) held a hearing to go over the nominations of Nicole Saphier to be surgeon general, Chris Klomp to be deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and Timothy Westlake to be assistant secretary for mental health and substance use.

Saphier, a radiologist and former Fox News contributor, is Trump’s third pick after his previous two failed to gain enough support among Senate Republicans. Klomp is a top ally of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. who is currently serving as HHS chief counselor and was credited with leading implementation of the Trump administration’s “ most favored nation ” policy.

Westlake, a board-certified emergency physician, currently serves as chief of staff at the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA).

In contrast to prior confirmation hearings for Trump’s health nominees, Wednesday’s hearing was notably tame. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle signaled an openness to the nominees before them.

Here are three takeaways from Wednesday’s hearing:

Klomp and Westlake both have some familiarity with members of the committee through their work for the administration, with Klomp having appeared before the Senate Finance Committee on Tuesday to discuss his nomination.

Both Saphier and Westlake have backgrounds in supporting legislative priorities that align with those of the committee members.

Saphier, director of breast imaging at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center-Monmouth, helped draft and pass state-level legislation that mandated breast density notification to patients while practicing in Arizona, later supporting similar policies in states like New York and New Jersey.

Dense breast tissue can make it harder for traditional mammograms to detect potential cancers. Past research suggests most women don’t know about their breast density or about the association to higher breast cancer risk.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) noted during the hearing that she and Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wis.) have introduced legislation to reauthorize the National Breast and Cervical Cancer Early Detection Program, and she told Saphier that she looked forward to working with her on better implementing the program.

Last year, Westlake testified in support of the HALT Fentanyl Act, the legislative framework for which he helped develop first in 2016 in Wisconsin. The bill outright classifies all fentanyl-related substances as Schedule I controlled substances, in lieu of scheduling each fentanyl-related substance separately.

HELP Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) praised Westlake’s help in supporting the legislation.

“I’m confident that you will continue to champion and promote pro-patient policies as assistant secretary for mental health and substance use,” said Cassidy.

A less combative Trump health nominee hearing

The energy during Wednesday’s hearing was not as tense as previous hearings have been, perhaps due to the lower profile nature of the positions for which the nominees are up for, as well as their more mainstream backgrounds.

Cassidy offered a warm reception to the nominees during the hearing, saying he “really enjoyed all of your opening statements.”

The senator from Louisiana was further heartened when Saphier said the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine was “our greatest tool for combating measles.” She also said the vaccine is not lethal — a departure from Trump’s recent remarks about the shot .

Saphier likely won some more points with Cassidy when she voiced her support for a universal birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine, a policy that Trump and Kennedy have both opposed and an issue close to Cassidy’s heart.

“I’m open to future discussions about it, but at this point, the data that we have is based on the universal birth dose. And being someone in academic medicine, I believe in evidence-based medicine, and that’s all I have right now is that the universal birth dose has been the most effective policy here in the United States for reducing infection,” Saphier said.

Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.) similarly offered a warm welcome to the nominees, congratulating Klomp on his nomination.

More direct responses on Trump, vaccine questions

The nominees on Wednesday were noticeably less evasive than previous Trump picks, giving mostly unequivocal answers to questions posed by lawmakers.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle expressed frustration with vague, conditional remarks that previous nominees had given the committee.

When pressing Saphier for more robust support of MMR vaccines, Cassidy said, “I’ve had wiggle room from people sitting there, as Senator Baldwin said, who later used that wiggle room to do things which were quite contrary.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) said, “We’ve had previous nominees come before the committee that stated their intention to preserve scientific integrity and independence. Multiple times, we’ve seen this not that commitment not being upheld.”

Sen. Maggie Hassan (D-N.H.) asked both Saphier and Westlake, “If directed by the president to take action that would break the law, would you follow the law or follow the president’s directive?”

Similar questions were posed to previous health nominees like former Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Director Susan Monarez and current National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya. In both instances, Bhattacharya and Monarez insisted that Trump would never ask them to break the law.

In contrast, Saphier and Westlake each answered without appealing to Trump.

Saphier told Hassan, “I have no intention of breaking the law, senator,” while Westlake said, “My ultimate responsibility is to the American people. I follow the law.”

Trump is hands-off on Houthis and the Saudis aren’t happy

President Trump is taking a notably hands-off approach as Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen rapidly gain ground in their bid to secure a Red Sea choke point.

© Abdulnasser Alseddik, Associated Press

The Houthis’ advances could further roil global energy markets and box in Saudi Arabia, but Trump has reportedly rebuffed a request from Riyadh to launch strikes on the group. The U.S. has instead sent advisers to support the kingdom, which also saw key energy pipelines attacked in recent days.

Vice President Vance said Monday that while the U.S. has been “keeping pretty close tabs” on the situation, officials are “ going to keep on monitoring it , and making sure that America’s best interests are represented.”

On Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee insisted the fighting is “ really not a big expansion ” of the larger U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, noting the Houthis have refrained from hitting American targets.

“In this case I don’t think it’s quite that bad,” Huckabee said of the Houthis’ actions on Newsmax. “What we do have is a for sure skirmish between Saudi Arabia and Yemen , but it has not really gone across the region. … That’s the good news.”

The approach marks a stark contrast to the early days of the Trump administration, when the president in March 2025 ordered strikes on the Houthis in response to attacks on shipping vessels in the Red Sea — plans that were famously shared by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on a Signal chat that included The Atlantic’s editor in chief.

But the U.S. is reluctant to step into the fray this time around, given its insistence that Washington has all but wrapped up its fighting with Tehran, a narrative to be further called into question should a new battleground open up, according to analysts.

“War with the Houthis right now would counter [Trump’s] narrative that this conflict is essentially over,” said Jeffrey Feltman, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution think tank.

“It would be inconvenient to the reality he’s trying to project that there’s nothing to see there anymore, that the war is basically over. It’d be hard to sustain that narrative if you’re suddenly opening a second front,” he told The Hill.

Trump donor Harold Hamm’s oil company Continental Resources announced a deal Wednesday to drill in Venezuela.

Continental signed a memorandum of understanding with Venezuela’s state-run oil company that would allow it to operate in a 126,000 acre-area of the oil-rich Orinoco Belt, according to a press release .

“Continental was built to recognize great resource opportunities and have the conviction to pursue them,” Hamm said in a written statement.

“What this company is doing today builds on that foundation while taking Continental to an entirely new level. I could not be more proud of the company, our people and the future we are building,” he added.

The deal announcement comes on the heels of separate deals announced by the U.S. government and Chevron in Venezuela in recent weeks.

It follows the Trump administration’s incursion into Venezuela earlier this year and capture of leader Nicolás Maduro.

After that invasion, Trump pushed U.S. oil companies to invest in producing oil in the South American nation that’s estimated to have large quantities of oil.

Meanwhile, Hamm donated large amounts of money to Trump’s presidential campaigns. He’s also one of the donors to President Trump’s ballroom project.

articles.body:
The House on Tuesday passed a bill aimed at shielding Americans from increased electricity costs associated with data centers.

The bill requires states to consider taking up standards that would force tech companies to shoulder the electricity cost increases associated with large data centers but doesn’t actually require them to regulate.

The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act , sponsored by Reps. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.) and Gabe Evans (R-Colo), passed 417-3 under a fast-track process known as suspension of the rules.

The vote comes at a moment of rising backlash to both artificial intelligence itself and the data centers that power it .

The legislation describes a framework under which facilities that demand a lot of electricity — like large data centers — would be charged a rate that would cover the full cost of any additional power production or electricity infrastructure required to meet their demand so that costs do not fall on the general public.

It does not force state regulators to adopt the framework but says states must hold a hearing on such a policy within two years of the bill’s enactment.

The bill’s supporters describe it as a solid push that could ultimately spur state-level action to protect consumers.

“The Ratepayer Protection Act helps to safeguard these benefits by ensuring that the companies who are building data centers — and not American families and small businesses — are paying for the electricity they use,” said Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) in a statement. “U.S. leadership in the race to AI dominance is critical to our economic prosperity and national security, so we need to keep building the needed infrastructure with appropriate accountability measures.”

Critics, however, say it is toothless and may not spur significant changes at a time when AI data centers threaten to drive up electricity costs and destabilize the grid .

Progressive Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.) posted to social media ahead of the vote, writing that she was not supporting the bill that “fails to meaningfully protect our communities.”

“The strongest action Congress can take right now is to pass a national moratorium on data centers and enact a prohibition on federal lands,” she wrote.

While the bill has broad bipartisan support, its future was not immediately clear. Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) introduced a companion bill in the Senate, but it has not yet gotten a vote.

Husted spokesperson Olivia Tripodi said via email that the senator is happy the House is moving the bill this week and “is having conversations on how the Senate can follow suit.”

Allison Clements, a former member of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), said that if it becomes law, the bill could be a good step, but for some states, the requirement could be redundant of what they are already forced to do by a recent commission order .

“Is it a good step? Yes. Is it anywhere close to sufficient relative to these challenges? No,” Clements, a Democrat who is now principal at energy consulting firm 804 Advisory, said of the bill.

“It’s going to be duplicative in a lot of states,” she said, but noted that states that are not covered by the FERC order “will be required to at least open a proceeding at the state level to think about these issues.”

articles.title: Trump slams the Fed rate hike, says he told Warsh 'you might as well vote with the board'
articles.summary: President Trump reacted to Wednesday's interest rate increase by saying rates "in the United States should be 1%, or less."
articles.body:
President Trump reacted to Wednesday's Fed rate hike , saying "Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less" and acknowledging he discussed with Kevin Warsh the Fed chair's plans for how to vote ahead of time.

"I talked to Kevin and I said, 'you might as well vote with the board because it's not going to matter,'" Trump told reporters Wednesday evening.

The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously Wednesday to raise rates by 25 basis points, its first hike in three years and the first under Warsh.

The president, who has spent more than a year calling for lower rates, first posted on Truth Social that rates should be dropping and that the trade deficit was a reason to "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" days after he threatened to stop trading with countries that have a trade deficit unless the Fed cuts rates.

Later Wednesday, when he was asked by reporters if he still has confidence in Warsh, Trump said he did, but said "he's got a very tough board." He called the FOMC "a bunch of politicians."

In a press conference Wednesday afternoon, Warsh demurred on the question of presidential involvement in the Fed decision, telling reporters, "I've got nothing for you on a discussion with the president."

Trump's suggestion of his own role in the voting process came after the White House tried to telegraph a hands-off approach to the Federal Reserve in recent weeks, but saw Trump and his team quickly hit back at the decision repeatedly.

Senior Deputy press secretary Kush Desai also reacted to the move in an appearance on Fox News, calling it a "rather unfortunate decision by the Federal Reserve" that was "not backed by a particularly compelling economic case."

Trump has now repeatedly praised Warsh personally while also calling the FOMC "political" for not lowering rates. Just this past weekend, the president also again stated his view that the US should have the lowest interest rates in the world.

Warsh voted along with all of his colleagues on the committee to raise rates but didn't offer a projection about future rate hikes and dodged questions about politics and the president multiple times.

He called independence of the central bank a "two-way street."

"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane…we'll let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too," he said.

The central bank also signaled that one more rate hike is likely before the end of the year, an acknowledgment that the Fed needed to step in to counteract price pressures.
